title: Roseville resident recounts flash flooding as creek overflow leaves long road to recovery
text:

The water has receded in Perry County after a devastating round of flash flooding, but for hundreds of displaced residents, the long road to recovery is just beginning.
More than 380 people have been displaced as community groups, the Red Cross and more than 40 agencies work to help families, restore power and assess the damage. For residents who watched floodwaters rise to unprecedented levels, the cleanup comes with uncertainty about when, or whether, they will be able to return home.
In Roseville, David Grannon said he watched water rise higher than he had ever seen as it rushed down his street, leaving him unable to get out of his driveway.
“It’s kind of scary I thought especially when it got higher and I'd never seen it get that high before,” Grannon said. Water coming that way and water going that way across the bridge. It just made a mess. Although the water has receded, damage remains visible along W. Athens Road outside Roseville, where chunks of asphalt were ripped out of the roadway and standing water lingered in areas hit by the storm.
In Crooksville, more than 380 people are displaced, including Kassidy Adams, who shared cellphone video showing damage near her apartment. Adams said she and her boyfriend escaped through deep water.
“Me and my boyfriend had to jump off the porch and it was like neck deep. It was like me and him were swimming in a lake to get to where we could finally stand up and get to safety,” she said. In a video she shared assessing the damage near her home, Adams can be heard reacting to the scene: “This is bad. Bad bad bad.
” Now, crews are conducting secondary searches of homes and working to restore power, making sure no one who may need help has been missed. But as Perry County shifts from emergency response to cleanup, residents are worried about what comes next. Adams said residents at her apartment complex have been told they are responsible for dealing with the aftermath themselves.
“They’re telling all of the tenants that they’re on their own and that they’re not responsible to help us because we knew what we were getting into when we moved in there,” she said. “She keeps saying 'I want to go home' and I’m like 'Well honey we can’t go home right now,'" Adams said. "You know I don’t know when we’ll be able to go home again. ” Gov.
Mike DeWine and the State Emergency Management Agency said recovery in Perry County will not happen overnight and could take weeks, with some families needing help for much longer. Officials are asking people to document damage, outline what they have lost and answer questions from assessors as the process continues. DeWine said he is working with the attorney general to make sure renters are given a reasonable timeline to collect their belongings and are not left with nowhere to go.
"You may never be able to go back to your apartment or to your house, and you don’t even know what’s salvageable at this point,” DeWine said. The extent of federal assistance will depend in part on the severity of the damage and the total amount of losses. Officials say that if the damage does not meet the threshold for federal assistance, the state is also exploring other ways to help affected residents.
Longer-term assistance could also come through the governor’s office and the state Legislature. For residents in communities like Roseville, the hope now is simple: that the water never rises this high again.
